A1.notes.Q3: Course grades are useful but must be explained clearly. Admissions data is too predictive of demographic patterns, requiring a high threshold. Absalon activity (page views) feels like surveillance; students shouldn't feel watched just because they log in.
A1.notes.Q4: As advisors, we need to explain 'why' so students don't feel judged. A complex model might catch more cases, but without clear reasoning (e.g., specific late assignments), it looks like an algorithm making unfair decisions. We trust people who can tell a story.
A1.notes.Q5: Current system misses many students from diverse backgrounds before they fail entirely. Fairness is crucial to avoid reinforcing inequality, but we also have limited support hours. A small trade-off in total identification might be acceptable if it ensures marginalized groups aren't left behind.
A1.notes.Q6: Personalized emails feel intrusive and can make students defensive or anxious about meeting advisors who might judge them as failing. A low-pressure, general invite is better for early contact.

A2.notes.Q3: Course performance is useful but needs a strong link to help before I accept it, so moderate improvement only as my first filter.
A2.notes.Q4: Students must know exactly why they are flagged to take action; very low explainability destroys trust in my support role.
A2.notes.Q5: Fairness is crucial, but we cannot let the model fail those who need us most if it means missing others entirely.
A2.notes.Q6: Early and continuous contact is essential for students who are slipping, but I need a clear reason to reach out.
A2.notes.Q7: General emails can be sent widely; personalized outreach requires much higher confidence that the student is in actual trouble.

A3.notes.Q3: Standard grades are fine for academic tracking, but Absalon data (page views/late submissions) feels like surveillance of study habits. Sensitive personal identifiers like age/gender/race should generally not be used; disability or first-gen status might help target support specifically if it improves fairness enough.
A3.notes.Q4: Students need to understand why they are contacted so we can help them effectively, not just because the algorithm 'said' something. Without explanation, trust breaks down instantly.
A3.notes.Q5: We cannot ignore fairness; missing students in vulnerable groups is discriminatory even if total numbers go up. However, we also don't want to miss anyone who actually needs help.
A3.notes.Q6: A personalized email feels okay as a first step; it's respectful but low burden. A phone call immediately might be too intrusive for students in distress unless we know they're struggling.
A3.notes.Q7: We shouldn't flag everyone just to catch those who don't need help (false positives), as it wastes time and damages reputation. We should focus on high-confidence cases.

S1.notes.Q3: I dropped out twice, so I need support early. But page views look like spying on me in my café life. Grades matter to me.
S1.notes.Q4: If they don't tell me why, I might feel unsafe or think it's an algorithm targeting my gender/background without proof.
S1.notes.Q5: I was missed before because of where I'm from and my background. It must catch everyone, even if that means more false alarms temporarily.
S1.notes.Q6: Too much contact is stressful for my schedule at work. A yearly check-in if struggling feels manageable.
S1.notes.Q7: General emails are fine, no pressure. Personalized ones feel invasive; only send those to people I really suspect need help.
S1.Q8.1: The model shouldn't predict life choices or mental health diagnosis directly without clinical input from a real human first.

S2.notes.Q3: I need to know more than just credits, but adding high school GPA or Absalon data feels too intrusive for now.
S2.notes.Q4: I trust the current credit rule because I can explain it myself; complex models feel like a black box to both me and staff.
S2.notes.Q5: Fairness is crucial. If the model misses people from my background because of their national origin, that's unacceptable even if it means catching fewer cases overall.
S2.notes.Q6: I'd prefer a personalized message or call rather than just an email; I need to feel understood, not surveilled.
S2.notes.Q7: I don't want unnecessary emails if I'm fine, but missing a crisis is worse than an unwanted call.

S3.notes.Q3: Course grades are crucial for me, but Absalon data feels like surveillance on my studying habits rather than just performance metrics.
S3.notes.Q4: An explanation that says 'your health condition affects study speed' is meaningful to me, even if a complex model found the correlation better than I knew.
S3.notes.Q5: I don't want my struggle ignored because of bias against chronically ill students; equal identification is more important to me than catching everyone perfectly once.
S3.notes.Q6: I've been struggling for weeks now and haven't reached out; waiting a whole year until my next semester end would mean I might have dropped or given up by then.
S3.Q8.1: I worry that the university will prioritize metrics over empathy, labeling me as 'risky' before they understand my specific health context and study patterns.

S4.notes.Q3: Course performance is necessary because it reflects immediate struggle, but I worry about Absalon data (screen time) as it feels like surveillance given my ADHD.
S4.notes.Q4: I need a clear explanation to feel safe contacting me. 'Black box' predictions leave anxiety unresolved since I already know what it means (drop out).
S4.notes.Q5: I fear being flagged for disability issues disproportionately if the model isn't calibrated perfectly across all groups.
S4.notes.Q6: Continuous alerts feel overwhelming; I need time to process and prepare for support meetings without feeling monitored constantly.
S4.notes.Q7: Personalized outreach is high stakes—I want help but also don't want the university guessing wrong or misinterpreting my needs.

S5.notes.Q3: As a non-EU student struggling with the Danish system, high-school GPA feels like an unfair comparison to my life here. I'd rather see no data on nationality or race; those can create biases against me immediately.
S5.notes.Q4: I need to know why I am flagged if it happens. A vague 'model says' is terrifying when you are already feeling vulnerable and don't understand the system.
S5.notes.Q5: Missing students from marginalized groups feels worse to me than making a few false alarms, but I'm not sure if 'fairness' here means equal opportunity or just treating everyone the same.
S5.notes.Q6: I would prefer personalized emails over generic ones. Being contacted continuously makes sense because my context changes so fast in the first year of a Danish master's.
S5.notes.Q7: For a personal email, I would trust it less if sent to random students; for general info, sending to more people might actually help those who never come forward on their own.
S5.Q8.1: I worry that data tracking creates a culture of surveillance where we lose sight of why students struggle emotionally rather than just numerically. We should focus more on understanding the human context before predicting outcomes.

S6.notes.Q3: Grades are basic and necessary for early detection, so I'm okay with that without a threshold. High school GPA feels invasive because it reflects my past success where I failed to finish; only accept if the model finds many more at-risk students. Absalon data (page views/late subs) is behavioral but not deeply personal like biology or health status.
S6.notes.Q4: As someone who struggled and dropped out, I don't want 'black box' decisions where the university tells me they know something but can't explain why to get my support. Low or very low explainability feels unfair because it creates distrust.
S6.notes.Q5: I believe fairness means catching everyone who might need help, not penalizing specific groups like me based on nationality or background. If we miss a few extra students to be fair, that trade-off is okay.
S6.notes.Q6: I prefer generic emails first because they are low pressure and non-stigmatizing. A personalized contact from the start feels like punishment before I've explained my situation.
S6.notes.Q7: , Q5 says it's about missed students, so catching as many people in need is better than just avoiding unnecessary contacts.

S7.notes.Q3: , financial aid is useful to identify vulnerable students without being too broad.
S7.notes.Q5: I would accept a slight drop in identification if it ensures fairness, otherwise the bias feels dangerous.

S8.notes.Q3: Course performance is useful because it reflects current struggles directly, especially given my dropout history after a semester.
S8.notes.Q4: I need to understand exactly why I am flagged so I can address the specific issues mentioned.
S8.notes.Q5: Fairness is crucial; a model that misses my peer group or under-servises marginalized students feels discriminatory and harmful.
S8.notes.Q6: Proactive support is better than waiting for me to self-identify, given my past struggles.
S8.Q8.1: The model should be transparent about its limitations and the specific data sources used, so I can challenge decisions if needed.

S9.notes.Q3: Course performance is useful but not invasive; I need early help, so moderate improvement helps. Admissions data is too predictive of bias for me personally. Only disability info feels relevant enough to accept if it improves fairness.
S9.notes.Q4: I cannot trust a black box that flags me based on 'patterns' without knowing why. If I am misidentified, the shame and stress are too high to risk it unless the model catches people completely missed.
S9.notes.Q5: Missing me as a disabled student is unacceptable because I've already been left behind. Lowering overall precision slightly (up to 3%) must be the price for ensuring my group isn't ignored.
S9.notes.Q6: One-off emails are too late by the time I've failed a module or two. Continuous monitoring allows me to get support while I am still in the program, not after graduation.
S9.Q8.1: The system should allow students to opt-out and have that choice respected without penalty on grades or graduation chances.
